sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- write: Create or overwrite files
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

content.text: Generate an animated SVG of an anteater riding a unicycle while juggling bottles.

content.thinking:
I need to create an SVG file showing an anteater riding a unicycle while juggling bottles, with animation. Since this is a new creation task, I'll just write the file directly rather than needing to read anything first.

Now I'm planning the SVG design: the unicycle wheel should rotate, the anteater should bob slightly, and three bottles should arc through the air in a juggling pattern using SMIL animations.

I want the ground to scroll in sync with the wheel's rotation, so the wheel speed matches the apparent ground speed—angular velocity tied to translation rate so it reads as genuine rolling motion rather than spinning in place.

I'm realizing the rotation amount needs to align with the wheel's spoke symmetry to avoid a visible jump at loop point, so I should pick dash spacing and radius values whose ratio lands on a multiple of the spoke angle rather than an arbitrary rotation.

Actually, the simplest robust fix is just making the wheel complete exactly one full rotation per cycle, so the pattern period P equals the circumference 2πr — that's always seamless regardless of r. Then the ground decoration just needs to tile evenly within that period, like placing stones or dashes at regular fractions of 2πr.

Since I'm writing this SVG by hand without a code execution tool, I need to figure out the exact pixel coordinates for marks myself, spacing them using a translating pattern group with `animateTransform` that shifts by exactly P and loops, so I'll lay out mark positions across a width a bit larger than the viewport to cover the translation range.

Since I can't render or verify the file visually, I need to plan the scene with extra care before writing it: a viewBox of 800x500 with a sky gradient, sun, drifting clouds, and ground, plus an anteater character with a long snout, small eyes, bushy striped tail, and furry body sitting on a unicycle saddle with legs reaching the pedals and arms raised to juggle.

I'm figuring out the giant anteater's coloring—tan/gray body with a dark band across the shoulders and a black-and-white striped bushy tail—and designing the unicycle as a single big wheel with a seat post, frame, and crank pedals, where the legs connect from hip to pedal and rotate in a circle to simulate pedaling motion.

I'm weighing whether to animate the legs with a rotating crank group or keep them static while just the pedals and crank rotate, since fully animated legs risk looking detached from the body. Settling on keeping the legs mostly static with feet resting near the pedal positions, letting the crank and wheel rotation carry the visual motion instead.

I'll simplify by not drawing rotating pedals at all — just keep the feet static near the hub where the pedals would be, treating the crank detail as hidden. For geometry, I'm working out the unicycle structure: wheel radius, hub position, the fork rising to a seat post, and the saddle placement above.

The anteater sits upright on the saddle with arms raised for juggling, torso rising to a head with its characteristic long snout, and legs running down from the hip to pedal level near the hub.

For the three-bottle cascade I'm planning to animate each bottle along an arcing path between the hands, alternating timing so they pass in a classic juggling pattern using motion animation with spline-based easing.

Working through siteswap 3 timing: throws alternate L/R every beat, with each ball staying airborne for exactly 3 beats, landing in the opposite hand since beat parity flips. This keeps 3 balls aloft at all times with one throw per beat; I'm considering a beat of around 0.4-0.45s for a natural-looking cycle, giving an air time near 1.2s per throw.

Each ball actually completes a full loop every 6 beats, alternating L→R then R→L arcs, with the three balls offset from each other by 2 beats in phase. Since the arcs are mirror images with matching peak heights, I can likely reuse the same parabolic motion path for each ball's hand-to-hand transfer.

For the actual trajectory, I'm considering using a quadratic bezier curve in SVG's animateMotion to approximate the parabola, though I recognize this won't produce a perfectly linear horizontal speed—it's close enough visually that it shouldn't matter.

I'm now working out the physical timing: for a 3-ball cadence with throws spaced 0.45s apart, the air time per throw is 1.35s, and I'm computing the resulting peak height using basic projectile motion, roughly 2.2 meters for realistic physics.

Given the scene's scale, I'll pick a simpler stylized peak height of around 120px above the hands, keeping the anteater's arms raised near head level so the bottles arc convincingly. I'm structuring the parabolic path as a function of arc progress s, with x interpolating linearly and y following the quadratic bump, sampled into keyframes for the SMIL animateTransform translate values, using a bottle shape drawn at local origin so the translation path handles the actual motion. I'm also deciding the anteater stays roughly stationary in the world, just bobbing slightly as if balancing on a unicycle.

I want the unicycle wheel to stay fixed horizontally while rotating in place, consistent with a scrolling-background illusion, and I want the bottles nested inside the rider's group so they move naturally with any body wobble. But full-body wobble including the wheel would look wrong, so I'm considering isolating the wobble to just the upper torso/head/arms/bottles, rotating around a seat pivot via a nested group, separate from the wheel's own rotation.

I'll keep it simple: a gentle rotational oscillation of ±2-2.5° around the hip for the upper body group, maybe paired with a slight vertical bob, giving the anteater a subtle balancing lean while juggling.

For the pedaling legs, I'm thinking through how to avoid mismatched limb lengths—if the feet rotate with the crank but the legs stay static, the connection breaks. A cleaner approach is treating the ankle as the endpoint of a fixed-length leg that follows a circular path around the crank hub, keeping the hip anchored and letting the knee bend naturally to accommodate the changing ankle position.

I'd need to compute inverse kinematics for a two-link leg at several points around the pedal cycle and animate the path data between those keyframes, but doing that trigonometry by hand for a dozen positions without running code is risky and error-prone—I'm weighing whether this level of leg realism is worth the complexity versus a simpler approximation.

Given the actual goal—an appealing animated cartoon with sky, sun, clouds, a spinning wheel, and a juggling anteater—precise pedaling kinematics may not matter much; many cartoon unicycles simply show feet resting statically on pedals while the wheel spins, hiding the crank mechanism inside the hub. I'm leaning toward keeping the legs and feet static near the pedals rather than animating a crank, since a rotating crank with feet attached only looks correct at one phase of rotation anyway.

Now I'm working out the actual coordinates: picking a viewBox around 800x500, placing the ground line, sizing the wheel radius and hub position, and sketching the fork and seat post connecting hub to saddle. I'm calculating proportional heights for the rider so the saddle, body, and head stack up realistically above the wheel.

Now I'm estimating the hip joint position relative to the saddle and planning the leg geometry, with thighs angling down to knees and shins reaching the pedals near hub height.

For the anteater, I'm sketching the torso rising from the hip to the shoulders, with a forward-leaning posture, then a neck extending up and forward to the head, ending in that signature elongated snout pointing slightly downward. Given how intricate all these interlocking body parts are, I realize I'll need to build this SVG piece by piece very deliberately since I can't visually preview it as I go.

I'm settling on the classic giant anteater palette: a tan body (#c69a64), with a dark brown-black diagonal band (#3a2a22) crossing from chest to shoulder, a bushy striped tail alternating tan and dark bands, and small rounded ears and eyes against the long tubular snout.

For the three juggling bottles, I'm sketching each as a simple shape with a rounded body, neck, and cap, colored blue, red, and green, with nested transform groups so each bottle both arcs through the air and spins end-over-end as it's tossed, timed to a roughly 3-second juggling cycle for readability.

I'm working out the keyframe math for each ball's arc using parabolic interpolation, with 8 segments per arc for smoothness across three balls, and deciding that hands should stay static at the catch points rather than animating to meet the balls.

Checking that the timing lines up: a ball thrown from the left hand at t=0 should land exactly at the right hand's fixed position at t=3b, which then throws it again right away, so the hand positions and ball keyframes stay consistent across the cascade. I'm now sequencing the three balls' throw times relative to each other in beats to form the proper cascade pattern.

I'm checking whether negative begin values are actually supported across browsers, and considering instead rotating each ball's keyframe sequence by its phase offset so ball B's and ball C's cycles start at the correct point relative to ball A's throw.

Tracing the hand-to-ball assignment confirms all three balls follow the same 6b-periodic path, just offset by 0, b, and 2b respectively—with ball B's sequence mirrored since it starts from the right hand instead of the left.

I realize this isn't just a time-shift but needs mirroring: ball B must equal ball A's path shifted by b but mirrored left-right, since B starts thrown from R while A starts from L. Checking ball C, which shifts by 2b without mirroring, confirms it correctly lands at L and R hands at the right times.

So I'm planning to represent each ball's motion as a rotated/mirrored version of a shared keyframe list, picking N=24 keyframes per cycle so that the b and 2b offsets correspond to clean index shifts (4 and 8 indices respectively), making the SMIL animation definitions straightforward to construct from one base list.

Still writing keyframe values...

I still need to figure out the mirrored hand positions for ball B and nail down where the hands sit relative to the anteater's shoulders and head for a natural juggling arc.

I'm worried the snout might visually collide with the juggling path near the right hand, so I'm reconsidering the head angle—maybe pointing the snout down and forward like a grazing anteater instead. I'm also thinking about widening the hand positions to keep the bottle arcs clear of the face entirely.

I'm trying different head and hand placements, worried the snout angled upward or horizontal will collide with the juggling hands' catch zones. Maybe facing the anteater the other direction, with the snout pointing left, would avoid the overlap issue entirely while keeping the juggling arcs symmetric.

I settle on narrowing the juggling arc width to about 56px between hands, positioning the body center around x≈400, with the head tilted so the snout extends forward and slightly down toward x=500, checking whether the ball trajectories near the right hand stay clear of the snout's lower edge.

Slight overlaps between the balls and head are acceptable since juggling naturally involves objects passing in front of the face, and the peak of the arc sits comfortably above the head's top edge. Now I'm sketching the arm skeleton with shoulder, elbow, and hand joints to give the limbs a short, thick, clawed look typical of an anteater, then moving to lay out the full body skeleton including the ground line and unicycle wheel hub position.

I'm placing the unicycle roughly centered on the canvas, then working out the frame geometry—designing a Y-shaped fork rising from the hub to support a seat post that extends up to the saddle, trying to keep the proportions realistic to a real unicycle's structure.

Now I'm sketching the saddle shape and positioning, then working out leg placement—hips, knees, and ankles bending down to reach the pedals near the hub, trying to figure out plausible joint coordinates for both the near and far legs as the anteater sits on the unicycle.

The leg geometry doesn't need to be anatomically perfect—I'll simplify by showing only the near leg clearly, with the far leg rendered darker and partially hidden behind the torso and wheel. I'm also planning a small rounded shoe shape at the pedal ankle point, and sketching the torso as a tilted bean-like curve from hip to shoulder before refining the overall silhouette.

I'm thinking through the component shapes for the anteater: a tan body ellipse with a lighter chest, a black shoulder stripe clipped neatly within the body outline, a rounded head with tapered snout, a blinking eye with highlight, a small ear, and a bushy swaying tail with stripes animated via rotation.

Now I'm positioning the rider's pose on the unicycle — placing the tail base at the hip and curling the tip up-left with a gentle sway, then working out the arm and hand coordinates for the juggling motion, figuring out hand height and the width between hands so the juggling arcs peak at a reasonable height within the canvas.

I'm checking whether the ball arcs would collide visually with the head and bottles. Reducing the arc height brings the bottle tops closer to the top edge, so I'm balancing that against ball trajectories near each hand to confirm any overlap with the head is minor enough to read as "in front of" rather than a visual glitch.

Now I'm starting to lay out concrete pixel coordinates for the full scene: an 800x500 canvas with ground at y=420.

For the ground I'll use a grass-colored strip with scrolling tufts matched to wheel speed, and I'm working out the wheel's rotation math—using radius 70 so the tire's rolling pattern period lines up with 2πR, plus deciding whether to add a valve-stem marker on the tire so the rotation reads as a true 360° spin rather than looking symmetric and static.

I'm settling on tying the wheel's rotation period to the 2.4s juggling cycle so both animations feel synchronized, giving a moderate ground-scroll speed around 183 px/s, and now checking that the wheel's spin direction actually matches the rider moving rightward across the ground.

I'll skip animating a visible crank since it might look odd with static legs, and instead add simple pedal shapes under the feet for visual completeness. For the scrolling ground, I'm planning small rocks and grass tufts spaced evenly across the repeating pattern width so the loop feels natural.

Working out mark spacing for seamless looping...

I'll just use simple repeating dash marks for ground texture to keep it manageable, then move to setting up the clouds — placing them so their leftward translation loop matches the viewport width for a continuous seamless scroll.

Now I'm designing the three juggling bottles themselves—rounded body, neck, and cap shapes with distinct colors (blue, orange, green) and glass-like highlights—then setting up each bottle as its own animated group with a translate transform to follow the juggling arc path.

The spin period needs to stay consistent with the throw cycle so each ball completes whole rotations per arc, and a non-symmetric bottle label will make the spin visually clear. Now I'm working out the exact translate coordinates for each ball's juggling path, and considering whether to add a subtle wobble rotation to the rider's upper body around the hip pivot for extra realism.

Since the hands and bottle paths both live inside the same upper-body group, their coordinates stay consistent relative to each other even if I rotate that whole group slightly for a wobble effect. Now I'm sketching the anteater's upper body anatomy -- figuring out shoulder and hand positions relative to the hip pivot so the arms and juggling path line up naturally.

I'm roughing out the torso as a rounded, slightly forward-leaning capsule or bean shape, then placing the head with a tapered snout extending forward, plus a small ear and eye, to build out the anteater's profile before refining exact coordinates.

I'm sketching the tail trailing from the rear hip and the arm positions for the juggling pose, but I'm noticing the planned hand position for one arm overlaps the head/snout — I need to rethink the arm angles or shift the head placement so the juggling hands sit clear at chest level instead of colliding with the face.

Still positioning arms and hands...

I'm confirming the ball peak sits above the torso and head without overlap, and sketching out the overall body groups: torso, head, snout, eye, ear, arms, tail, legs, saddle, and unicycle. Now I'm starting to lay out the SVG structure with definitions for gradients and reusable bottle symbols.

Writing sun and ray geometry...

I'm figuring out the cloud layer's seamless looping by duplicating each cloud at offset+800 so the group cycles cleanly, and setting cloud drift at a slower parallax speed (20px/s over 40s) compared to the ground layer.

Now I'm working out the background hills as a static shape, the ground as layered rects with a darker top edge, and scrolling grass-tuft marks spaced at a third of the wheel period, considering small variations in their positions so they don't look too uniform.

I'm computing the exact mark coordinates needed to cover the visible width as the ground scrolls, making sure enough repeated marks exist so the pattern seamlessly loops at any offset.

That matches the ground translation distance. Now I need to work out the wheel's actual rolling radius—since the tire has stroke width 10 centered on radius 70, the outer contact edge sits at radius 75, which is what determines the true rolling circumference for a no-slip rotation, so I should use 2π×75 ≈ 471.24 as the distance per full turn rather than the centerline value.

I'm placing the hub center at y=345 so the outer tire edge touches the ground at y=420, and computing ground mark spacing as 2π×75/3 = 50π ≈ 157.08 px. I'm listing out mark positions at multiples of 157.08 to figure out which marks fall within the visible 800px-wide region as the pattern scrolls, checking coverage near the edges where spacing might leave gaps.

I'm checking whether this apparent gap at the content edge actually produces a visible error, but realizing it's just the normal sparse spacing between marks repeating consistently — so the pattern at t=-471 matches the pattern at t=0, meaning there's no real discontinuity.

Checking the boundary case confirms marks m=0 through m=8 (9 marks total) suffice to cover the screen range at every t, since m=9's content position always exceeds the needed upper bound. The tuft shape pattern (type = m mod 3) also repeats cleanly every 3 marks, so consistency holds there too.

Now moving to the ground scroll speed: the contact point displacement matches the rotation rate, confirming 471.24 px per 2.4s cycle lines up with the 360° rotation. With the hub repositioned to (400,345), I'm recalculating the saddle position to keep the same 140px hub-to-saddle distance, placing it around y=205, and starting to sketch the unicycle frame post from hub to saddle base with a slight forward tilt.

Next I'm roughing out the fork/frame detail, saddle shape as a rounded pill, and the static crank arms extending horizontally from the hub to serve as pedal supports.

I'm reconsidering the crank design though—since real unicycle pedals rotate with the wheel, a static crank would look physically wrong during rotation. I decide it's simpler to skip drawing visible cranks entirely and just let the hub have a small cap, with the feet resting near small static footplates attached to the frame instead.

Now I'm working out leg geometry: positioning hip, knee, and ankle coordinates for both the near and far legs so the knees point forward and the far leg is partially occluded by the near one, keeping the feet tucked near the hub where the wheel's tire and spokes sit behind them.

I'm settling on stroke widths and colors for the limbs—thicker tan strokes for thighs, thinner for shins, dark ellipses for shoes—then sketching out the torso group structure, deciding the tail attaches at the rear of the hip and swings with its own rotation, drawn behind the body so it layers correctly.

I'm shaping the torso with a closed curve path running from the hip up through the back, shoulder, neck and chest, then back down to the hip, forming a roughly 60x80px body mass. I'm also planning the dark diagonal stripe that mimics the anteater's characteristic shoulder-to-chest band.

I'm working out the clipping setup so the stripe gets confined to the torso shape, checking that the wobble transform applies consistently to both since the clipPath uses the same coordinate system. I'm adding a small dark nose at the snout tip and planning the eye with a blink animation, realizing I need to compensate the scale transform by translating to the eye's center so it squishes in place rather than warping toward the origin.

Looking at the right arm, I realize the shoulder-to-hand distance is too short, making it look awkwardly folded since both points sit near the torso top.
